ingredients.note: Roast or raw, broken into a few pieces to fit the pot
Outer layer removed, bruised along their length, then halved
Whole, so they are easy to fish out
Half to be juiced, the rest cut into wedges for the table
Add at the end, as the ham and sauerkraut are salty

steps.text: Put the chicken carcass in a large pot with the water. Bring slowly to a gentle boil over a medium heat, skimming off any grey foam that rises to the surface.
Trim the lemongrass, peel away the tough outer layers, then bash each stalk with the back of a knife to bruise it. Halve the stalks and add them to the pot along with the star anise.
Reduce the heat to the lowest simmer, partly cover and cook for 45 minutes, until the broth smells perfumed and tastes rich. Do not let it boil hard or it will turn cloudy.
Meanwhile, halve the salad potatoes (quarter any large ones so the pieces are even) and dice the ham into 1cm pieces. Set both aside.
Lift out the carcass, lemongrass and star anise with tongs or a slotted spoon and discard. If any scraps of meat have fallen from the bones, pick them out and return them to the pot.
Add the potatoes to the strained broth and simmer for 15 to 18 minutes, until a knife slides in easily. Stir in the diced ham for the final 3 minutes just to warm it through.

Take the pot off the heat. Squeeze in the juice of half the lemon, then stir in the sauerkraut. Taste and season with salt and black pepper; go gently with the salt, as the ham and sauerkraut already carry plenty.
Ladle into two warmed bowls, dividing the potatoes and ham evenly. Cut the remaining lemon half into wedges and serve alongside so each person can add more brightness to taste.

tips: Add the sauerkraut and lemon juice off the heat so their fresh, tangy flavour stays bright rather than cooking away.
Keep the simmer barely bubbling for the clearest, most fragrant broth.
Leave the salt until the end and taste first, because the ham and sauerkraut both season the soup.

steps.text: Soak the dried wood ear mushroom in warm water for 20 minutes until soft and springy. Drain, trim off any hard knobbly bits and slice into thin strips.

Peel the sweet potato and cut into 2cm cubes. Cut the tinned ham into 1.5cm cubes. Peel the oro blanco, remove the pith and cut the segments free of their membranes, working over a bowl to catch the juice.
Heat the cooking oil in a medium pot over a medium-high heat. Add the ham and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning now and then, until the edges are browned and crisp.
Stir in the gochujang and cook for 1 minute until it darkens slightly and smells fragrant. Add the sweet potato and coat the cubes well in the paste.
Pour in the water and scrape up anything stuck to the base of the pot. Add the cinnamon stick, sultanas, sliced wood ear mushroom and black pepper. Bring to the boil.
Reduce the heat to low, partly cover and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sweet potato is just tender when pierced with a knife.

Stir in the sauerkraut and simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes more, until the sauce has reduced to a glossy coating and the sweet potato is soft but still holding its shape. Taste and add salt only if needed.
Remove the cinnamon stick. Fold in the oro blanco segments and any saved juice, and warm through for 1 minute. Serve hot in two bowls.

tips: If the stew thickens too much before the sweet potato is tender, add a splash of water and keep simmering.
Add more gochujang for extra heat, or less if you prefer the sweetness to lead.
Stir gently once the sweet potato softens so the cubes stay whole.

steps.text: If using dried wood ear mushroom, cover it with warm water and leave to soak for 20 minutes while you prepare everything else. Drain, rinse well, trim away any hard knobbly bits and slice into thin strips.

Put the salad potato chunks into a pan of cold water with a pinch of salt. Bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes until just starting to soften at the edges, then add the sweet potato cubes for the final 2 minutes. Drain well and leave to steam dry for a couple of minutes, which helps them crisp later.

Heat 2 tablespoons of cooking oil in a large, wide frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the drained potatoes in a single layer, season with salt and black pepper and leave undisturbed for 4 minutes so they form a golden crust. Turn and fry for a further 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until crisp and golden all over.

Push the potatoes to one side of the pan and add the guar beans and wood ear mushroom to the cleared space with a drizzle more oil. Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, tossing, until the beans are tender with a little bite and the mushroom is glossy.

Stir in the chopped kimchi and its juices, mixing everything together, and cook for 2 minutes until hot and the juices have reduced to a light coating. Taste, adjust the seasoning and divide between two warm bowls.

Wipe out the pan, return it to a medium heat and melt the butter. Crack in the eggs and fry for 2 to 3 minutes until the whites are set and crisp at the edges but the yolks are still runny, spooning a little hot butter over the whites.
Slide an egg onto each bowl. Scatter over the crumbled crowdie, sprinkle with dried parsley, add a final grind of black pepper and serve straight away.

tips: Dry potatoes thoroughly after boiling and avoid overcrowding the pan; this is the key to a really crisp finish.
Keep the yolk runny so it breaks over the bowl and acts as a rich sauce for the kimchi and potatoes.
Crowdie is mild and creamy, so it balances the tang and heat of the kimchi nicely.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan) and spread the frozen onion rings on a baking tray. Bake for 18 to 20 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crunchy. Keep them in the oven on low until you are ready to serve.

Melt the butter in a large, deep pan over a medium-low heat. Add the sliced leek with a pinch of salt and cook gently for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until completely soft and sweet but not browned.

Tip in the drained black-eyed peas and the water. Add the pepper and a little more salt. Bring to a gentle bubble, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then.
Press a few of the peas against the side of the pan with the back of a spoon to thicken the stew. If it looks too thick, add a splash of water. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

Meanwhile, heat the cooking oil in a frying pan over a medium heat. Toast the torn tortilla pieces in batches for 1 to 2 minutes each side until blistered, golden and lightly crisp at the edges. Drain on kitchen paper.
Take the stew off the heat and stir in the grated Manchego a handful at a time until it melts into the pot and the stew turns creamy and glossy.
Divide the toasted tortilla pieces between two warm, deep bowls. Ladle the stew over the top, then add the sliced avocado, a spoonful of mint yoghurt and a little chopped white kimchi.
Finish with the hot, crunchy onion rings on top and serve straight away, while the tortillas still have some bite.

tips: Wash the sliced leek in a bowl of cold water so any grit sinks, then lift it out and drain well.
Add the onion rings at the last moment so they stay crunchy rather than softening in the steam.
Manchego can turn stringy if boiled, so always stir it in off the heat.
Kimchi is tangy and salty, so taste the stew after serving it and add salt only if needed.

Cooked pie filling, broken into pieces
Trimmed and cut into short lengths

Go gently as the fillings are seasoned

steps.text: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan). Butter a medium baking dish generously, then scatter the semolina over the base and tilt the dish so it coats the sides too. Tap out any excess.

Melt half the remaining butter in a frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the girolles with a pinch of salt and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until their juices have cooked off and they are lightly golden.
Add the garlic to the girolles and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Tip everything out onto a plate and wipe the pan.
Melt the rest of the butter in the pan over a high heat. Add the guar beans and the water and stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes until just tender with a few browned spots. Season with black pepper.

Tear the croissants into rough chunks. Scatter half over the base of the prepared dish, then spoon over half of the chicken and mushroom pie, cheese and onion filling, girolles and beans, breaking the pie into pieces as you go.
Repeat with the remaining croissant and fillings, finishing with a few pieces of croissant on top so they catch and turn crisp.
Whisk the pancake mix with the milk until smooth, adding a pinch of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Pour slowly over the dish, pressing the croissant down gently so it soaks up the batter.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the batter is puffed, set and deep golden, and the filling is piping hot in the centre. Rest for 5 minutes before serving straight from the dish.

tips: Leave the dish to stand for a few minutes after pouring in the batter so the croissant soaks it up evenly.
If the top browns too quickly, cover the dish loosely with foil for the last 10 minutes.
Day-old croissant holds its shape best and gives the crispest edges.

steps.text: Put the bulgur wheat in a medium pan with the whole dried chilli, 300ml water and a good pinch of salt. Bring to the boil, cover, reduce to a very low heat and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes until the water is absorbed.

While the bulgur cooks, heat the cooking oil in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the bacon and fry for 3 to 4 minutes each side until golden and crisp. Lift onto a plate and keep warm, leaving the rendered juices in the pan.

Add half the butter to the same pan and let it foam. Tip in the girolles with a pinch of salt and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, tossing now and then, until they have softened and taken on some colour. Season with black pepper and move to the plate with the bacon.
Wipe the pan, add the remaining butter and lay in the fig quarters cut side down. Fry for 2 to 3 minutes until sticky and golden, then turn briefly and take off the heat.
Make the instant mash with about 300ml boiling water, following the packet directions, stirring until smooth and fluffy. Season with salt and black pepper.

Remove the chilli from the bulgur and fluff the grains with a fork. Spoon the mash into two bowls beside the bulgur, then top with the bacon, girolles and figs. Finish with a heap of raw sauerkraut and serve straight away.

tips: Leave the chilli whole and fish it out before serving for gentle warmth; leave it in longer for more heat.
Do not crowd the girolles in the pan or they will steam rather than brown.
Add the sauerkraut at the last moment so it keeps its sharp crunch.

steps.text: The night before, cover the kidney beans with plenty of cold water in a large bowl and leave to soak for at least 8 hours. Drain and rinse well before cooking.

Put the soaked beans in a saucepan, cover with fresh water and bring to a full, rolling boil. Boil hard for 10 minutes, skimming off any foam, then drain. This step is essential to make the beans safe to eat.
Warm the cooking oil in a heavy casserole over a medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and the whole cloves and cook for 1 to 2 minutes until the garlic is fragrant but not browned.

Add the boiled beans, the currants and 500ml of fresh water. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook slowly for about 1 hour 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beans are almost tender.

Stir in the tinned spaghetti in tomato sauce and the chopped kimchi with its juices. Add the black pepper. Simmer uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are completely soft and the stew is thick, sweet-sour and glossy. Add a splash of water if it becomes too dry.

Taste and season with salt. Fish out the whole cloves if you can find them. Nestle the pieces of perch fillet into the stew, spoon a little of the sauce over them, cover and cook very gently for 6 to 8 minutes until the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Ladle the stew and fish into two warm bowls, taking care not to break up the fillets. Top each bowl with a heap of curtido for a cool, crunchy finish and serve straight away.

tips: Never skip the hard 10-minute boil: raw or undercooked kidney beans are unsafe to eat.
Keep the simmer gentle once the perch goes in, so the fillets stay in large, tender flakes.
Add the curtido only at the table, so it stays crisp against the hot stew.

steps.text: Put the dried wood ear mushroom in a bowl and cover with the warm water. Leave for 20 minutes until soft and springy, then drain, trim off any hard knobbly bits and slice into thin strips.

Heat a grill or griddle pan to high. Brush the bars or pan lightly with the remaining cooking oil so the fish does not stick.
Melt the butter in a wide frying pan over a medium heat. Add the sliced leek with the salt and cook for 4 minutes, stirring, until starting to soften.
Add the chestnut mushrooms and the sliced wood ear to the leek. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the mushrooms have taken on some colour and released their juices.
Pour in the rose wine, bring to a simmer and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a glossy, buttery coating. Keep warm on a very low heat.

Lay the swordfish steaks on the hot grill and cook for 4 minutes without moving them, until golden and marked. Turn and cook for a further 3 to 4 minutes, until just cooked through and no longer translucent in the centre.

Place the whiting fillets skin side down on the grill. Cook for 3 minutes, then turn very gently and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more, until the flesh flakes easily. Whiting is delicate, so use a wide fish slice.
Arrange the swordfish and whiting on a warm platter. Spoon the rose wine mushrooms, leek and all the pan juices over the top and serve straight away for sharing.

tips: Fresh turmeric stains, so wear gloves or wash your hands and board straight after grating.
Swordfish dries out quickly, so take it off the heat as soon as the centre turns opaque.
Cook the whiting after the swordfish, as it needs far less time and is best served piping hot.

steps.text: Pat the lamb breast and turkey pieces dry and season them all over with salt and black pepper.
Heat the cooking oil in a large heavy casserole over a medium-high heat. Brown the lamb breast pieces well on all sides, then lift them out onto a plate. Pour off most of the fat.
Add half the butter to the same pot and brown the turkey pieces on all sides until golden. Return the lamb to the pot.
Stir in the grated fresh ginger for 30 seconds, then pour in the merlot, scraping up the browned bits from the base of the pot. Let it bubble for 3 minutes to cook off the sharpness.
Add the water, bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat to low. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and simmer very gently for 1 hour 15 minutes, until the meat is nearly tender.
Add the new potatoes, pushing them down into the liquid. Cover and simmer for 30 minutes more, until the potatoes are tender and the meat is falling from the bone.
Lift out the turkey pieces, pull the meat from the bones and discard the bones and skin. Return the meat to the pot, and skim any excess fat from the surface.

Stir in the red sauerkraut and the banana slices. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes, so the banana softens into the gravy and the sauce thickens slightly. Stir in the remaining butter and taste for salt and black pepper.
While the stew finishes, cook the frozen pakora according to the packet instructions until deeply crisp and golden.
Ladle the stew into two warm bowls and break the crisp pakora over the top just before serving, so they stay crunchy.

tips: Simmer the stew very gently; a hard boil makes the lamb breast and turkey tough and the gravy cloudy.
Use a firm banana rather than a very ripe one so the slices soften without disappearing completely.
The stew improves if made a day ahead; cook the pakora fresh just before serving.

steps.text: Peel and finely grate the fresh turmeric, and stone and roughly chop the green olives. Pat the minute steaks dry with kitchen paper and season both sides with salt and black pepper.
Toast the thick-cut white toast until golden and keep warm on the serving plates alongside the crispbread.

Heat the cooking oil and half the butter in the large frying pan over a high heat until foaming. Fry the steaks for about 1 minute on each side until well browned. Lift onto a plate and leave to rest.

Turn the heat down to medium. Add the grated turmeric to the same pan and stir for 30 seconds in the buttery juices until fragrant, then pour in the rose wine and scrape up all the sticky bits from the base of the pan.
Add the chopped green olives and the water. Simmer for 2 to 3 minutes until reduced by about half to a glossy golden sauce, then stir in the remaining butter and any juices from the resting steak.
Push the sauce to one side, add the baby spinach and turn it in the pan for about 30 seconds until just wilted. Season with a pinch of salt and black pepper.
Spoon the wilted spinach and golden sauce onto the plates, lay the steaks on top and scatter over the pumpkin seeds. Serve straight away with the toast and crispbread for scooping up the sauce.

tips: Rest the steaks while you make the sauce so they stay tender and the juices flow back into the pan.
Wear a thin glove or rinse your hands promptly after grating turmeric, as it stains skin and worktops.
Keep the pan hot for the steak: a minute steak is thin and overcooks in seconds.

steps.text: Pat the lamb dry and season with the pepper and a pinch of salt. Heat the oil and 20g of the butter in a wide, heavy casserole over a high heat until foaming. Brown the lamb in two batches for about 4 minutes each, until deeply golden on all sides, then lift out onto a plate.

Turn the heat to medium and add the remaining 10g of butter for the stew. Fry the galangal coins and girolles for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the mushrooms soften and smell nutty and the galangal turns fragrant.

Pour in the rose wine and scrape up all the sticky brown bits from the base. Let it bubble for 3 minutes, then return the lamb with its juices and add the water. Bring to a gentle simmer, partly cover and cook for 35 minutes, until the lamb is tender and the gravy has thickened slightly.

Stir the drained carrots into the stew and warm through for 3 minutes. Break the noodle blocks into large pieces and push them under the gravy, then sprinkle over the flavour sachets. Simmer for 3 minutes, turning once, until the noodles are just tender and have soaked up most of the gravy. Add a splash of carrot liquid or water if it looks dry.

Lay the Vacherin Fribourgeois slices over the top in an even, generous blanket. Cover with a lid, take off the heat and leave for 4 minutes, or slide under a hot grill, until the cheese is soft, glossy and melting into the noodles.

While the cheese melts, spread the cut sides of the hot cross buns with the last of the butter and toast them cut-side down in a dry frying pan for 2 minutes until golden. Spoon the stew into warm bowls and serve with the toasted buns on the side for mopping up the gravy.

tips: Brown the lamb in batches so it sears rather than steams; the colour is the flavour of your gravy.
Taste before adding salt at the end, as the noodle sachets and cheese both bring plenty.
If the cheese slides off the noodles, press it gently into the gravy with the back of a spoon as it softens.
Serve straight away while the noodles are still silky and the cheese is stretchy.

steps.text: Put the dried shiitake in a bowl and pour over 300 ml of hot water. Press them under the surface with a plate and leave to soften for about 20 minutes.

Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Spoon the choux paste into about 12 small mounds on a lined tray, well spaced. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until deep golden, risen and crisp. Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes.

Lift the shiitake from the bowl and squeeze them gently over it. Keep the dark soaking liquor, pouring it through a fine sieve to leave any grit behind. Discard the tough stalks and slice the caps thinly.

Add the sliced shiitake, the bruised lemongrass, the sieved soaking liquor and 400 ml of water. Bring to the boil, then lower the heat and simmer gently, partly covered, for 20 minutes until the broth is dark and fragrant.

Remove the lemongrass pieces from the broth. Season with salt and black pepper. Add the kamaboko slices and torn mozzarella and warm through for 2 to 3 minutes, until the mozzarella softens and begins to melt into strands.

Ladle the soup into two warm bowls. Float the choux puffs and crisp naan strips on top, add the last 10 g of butter in small knobs and finish with plenty of black pepper. Serve straight away so the puffs stay crisp.

steps.text: Whisk the chickpea flour with 1 tsp salt and the black pepper in a large bowl. Slowly pour in the cold pale ale, whisking until smooth, then rest the batter for 15 minutes. It should coat a spoon thickly; loosen with the water if it feels stodgy.
While the batter rests, pat the potato rounds dry and the tilapia strips dry. Season the tilapia with a pinch of salt and rub it with the grated ginger and the grated garlic clove.

Heat half the cooking oil in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. Fry the potato rounds in a single layer for 4 to 5 minutes each side until golden and crisp at the edges. Lift onto a plate and keep warm, leaving the oil in the pan.
Stir the sliced button mushrooms, torn oyster mushrooms and tilapia strips into the batter until everything is evenly coated.

Add the remaining oil to the pan and heat until a drop of batter sizzles at once. Spoon in the mixture in loose heaps, flattening each lightly. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and the fish is cooked through, working in batches and keeping the cooked fritters warm.

Wipe out the pan, then melt the butter over a low heat. Add the chopped garlic and a pinch of salt and cook gently for 1 minute until fragrant but not browned, then stir in a little extra grated ginger if you like.
Pile the fritters and crisp potato rounds onto warm plates and spoon the garlic and ginger butter over everything. Serve straight away.

tips: Keep the batter cold and do not overmix it, so the fritters stay light.
Dry the potato rounds well so they crisp rather than steam.
Fry in batches so the pan stays hot and the coating turns golden.

ingredients.note: trimmed of any sinew and cut into bite-sized pieces
outer layer removed, bruised with the back of a knife

steps.text: Pat the chicken livers dry and season them with a pinch of the salt and the black pepper. Cut the cep into thick slices and finely chop the garlic. Bruise the lemongrass along its length with the back of a knife.
Melt the butter in a large, deep frying pan or wide casserole over a medium-high heat until foaming. Add the cep slices and fry for 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until golden at the edges.
Add the chicken livers and fry for 2 minutes, turning, until browned outside but still pink within. Stir in the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Stir in the cayenne pepper and ground cinnamon, then pour in the chopped tomatoes and water. Add the bruised lemongrass and the remaining salt. Bring to the boil, scraping up any tasty browned bits from the base of the pan.

Tip in the orzo and stir well. Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer and cook, uncovered, for 12 to 14 minutes, stirring often so the orzo does not catch, until it is tender and the sauce turns thick and glossy. If it looks dry before the orzo is cooked, add a splash more water.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and black pepper. Fish out the lemongrass stalk and discard it. Rest the stew for 2 minutes, then serve hot in warm bowls.

tips: Do not overcook the livers; they should stay just pink in the middle so they remain tender and creamy.
Add the cayenne a little at a time, as the heat builds while the stew simmers.
Stir the orzo regularly as it cooks, since its starch thickens the sauce and can catch on the base of the pan.
